interest: This file offers valuable insight into how both Axis powers and Allied intelligence tracked and framed raw material resources during World War II, specifically the critical commodity of cotton. It vividly illustrates the sharp contrast between Axis wartime propaganda and economic reality: while German official media promoted an ambitious narrative that Japanese-occupied Southeast Asia would replace the United States as a global cotton supplier for Europe and Asia, Allied intelligence obtained direct admissions from Japanese domestic sources (Domei, The Oriental Economist, and Mainichi) conceding that cultivation in the Philippines and occupied China was negligible or stalled, and that a crippling shortage of merchant shipping left millions of tons of cargo immobilized. Additionally, the pre-war cross-reference concerning Anderson, Clayton & Co. sheds light on the commercial dilemmas facing major American private cotton exporters on the eve of the Pacific War.
overview: State Department decimal file 894.61321 (covering Japanese cotton and fiber crops) spans May 1941 to January 1943 and documents U.S. and Allied monitoring of Japanese cotton supply, commercial dealings, and wartime agricultural policies. The file begins with a May 1941 cross-reference to correspondence from the American cotton merchandising firm Anderson, Clayton & Co. regarding its trade with Japan prior to the Pacific War. The subsequent wartime documents focus on Axis economic propaganda and intelligence assessments regarding Japan's cotton cultivation in occupied territories. A September 1942 telegram from the U.S. Legation in Bern details German claims that Japan would convert sugar plantations in the Philippines and Celebes to cotton to supply European and Asian textile mills, a claim U.S. diplomats identified as German domestic propaganda designed to minimize perceived dependence on American supplies. An airgram from the U.S. Embassy in London in January 1943 transmits British Ministry of Information intelligence quoting Japanese sources (Domei, The Oriental Economist, and Mainichi) that refute these claims, acknowledging that cotton expansion in the 'Southern Region' had barely started, progress in occupied China was slow, and an acute shipping shortage had left twelve million tons of cargo stranded.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a letter from Anderson, Clayton & Co. discussing its cotton trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet indexing a letter dated May 17, 1941, from Anderson, Clayton & Co. (Fleming) filed under 694.1115/36. The letter presents facts concerning the firm's ongoing cotton trade with Japan and offers to discuss the situation further with the State Department. The reference is filed under decimal file 894.61321 (misnumbered in the stamp as 094.61321/1).
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Anderson, Clayton & Co. Cotton Trade with Japan

subfiles.about: Reports German economic propaganda alleging Japanese plans to cultivate cotton in Southeast Asia for export to Europe and Asia.
subfiles.summary: U.S. Minister Leland Harrison transmits a two-section telegram (No. 4014) from Bern detailing German official news agency (DND/DAD) reports regarding Japanese cotton expansion. The reports claimed that Japan planned to convert sugar cultivation to cotton in the Philippines, Celebes, and continental Asia to supply the Asian textile industry and export surplus raw cotton to Europe, while European nations would assist Japan with finished textiles. Harrison analyzes this dispatch as typical German economic propaganda designed to convince the German public that Europe could secure necessary raw materials in the postwar era without relying on American imports.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Harrison (Bern) on German Economic Propaganda Regarding Japanese Cotton Expansion

subfiles.about: Transmits British intelligence reporting Japanese admissions of lagging cotton cultivation and severe shipping bottlenecks.
subfiles.summary: U.S. Chargé d'Affaires H. Freeman Matthews in London forwards two intelligence items from the Far East Section of the British Ministry of Information to the Department of State. The first excerpt cites Domei and The Oriental Economist (quoted via Nachrichten für den Außenhandel) conceding that cotton cultivation in the Philippines is purely experimental, that Southern Region cotton expansion has barely started, and that progress in occupied China is sluggish. The second excerpt cites the Deutsche Bergwerkszeitung quoting Mainichi editor Shimoda, who highlighted acute economic disparities across the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere and disclosed that twelve million tons of cargo were marooned awaiting shipping.
subfiles.title: Airgram from Matthews (London) Transmitting British Intelligence on Japanese Cotton and Shipping Shortages
